shots.title: Plumbing everywhere
shots.engineer: Here are three services written in three languages. Each one carries its own networking plumbing: TLS, retries, timeouts, metrics and tracing, through whatever library exists for its language, at whatever version it last upgraded to. Orders retries three times with a two-second timeout. Payments calls catalogue over plain HTTP with no timeout at all. When the platform team needs one new security rule, they patch three code bases, and monitoring receives metrics in three different formats.
shots.executive: Every service does its own security, retries and monitoring in its own way, so one company-wide change means changing every service.

shots.title: Shared library
shots.engineer: The obvious fix is one shared library for mutual TLS and retries. The platform team writes it once, in Java, and orders upgrades and redeploys. Then someone ports it to Go by hand, and the Python port slips to next quarter. So orders talks to payments over mutual TLS, but payments still calls catalogue in plain text, and that call hangs because the port has no timeout. A library per language gives you several versions of the same idea, each released on its own schedule.
shots.executive: A shared code library has to be rewritten for every language and upgraded by every team, so the services never quite agree.

shots.title: Sidecar
shots.engineer: The sidecar pattern moves that plumbing into a separate process deployed next to every instance of the service. Microsoft describes it as attached to its parent and sharing its life cycle: created and retired together. In Kubernetes the sidecar is a second container in the same pod. Incoming calls reach the proxy first, over mutual TLS, and it hands them to the app on localhost. Outgoing calls go to the proxy too, which adds retries, timeouts and telemetry. The app keeps only business logic, in any language.
shots.executive: A small helper runs beside every copy of a service and handles security and networking for it, whatever language the service is written in.

shots.title: Control plane
shots.engineer: Put a sidecar proxy beside every service and you have a service mesh. The proxies are the data plane: they carry every request between services. A control plane manages them. In Istio, a component called istiod does service discovery, turns high-level routing rules into proxy configuration and pushes it out at runtime, and acts as a certificate authority, giving each workload an identity for mutual TLS. The platform team changes a rule once, and every proxy picks it up, with no redeploy of the services.
shots.executive: Together the helpers form a mesh. One central control plane hands them their rules and security certificates, so a change is made once for everyone.

shots.title: East-west
shots.engineer: Notice the two directions of traffic. A user's request comes in from outside through a gateway: that is north-south traffic, and an API gateway or ingress gateway owns it. Once inside, orders calls payments: that is east-west traffic, between services, and that is the mesh's main job. Each hop between pods is mutual TLS from proxy to proxy, while the hop from proxy to app stays on localhost. Both proxies report metrics and trace spans in the same format.
shots.executive: A gateway handles traffic coming into the system. The mesh handles the much larger volume of traffic between services inside it.

shots.title: Canary call
shots.engineer: Step by step. The control plane has already sent the orders sidecar its routes, say ninety per cent to payments version one and ten per cent to a canary of version two, plus its certificate. Orders makes an ordinary HTTP call to payments, on localhost. Its sidecar opens mutual TLS to the payments sidecar, and each side checks the other's identity. The reply comes back. The next request may land on the canary. Every call is recorded with latency, status and a trace span.
shots.executive: The service makes a plain call. The mesh encrypts it, checks who is on each end, sends a small share to a new version, and records everything.

card.heading: What the mesh adds, with no code change
points: Mutual TLS and a workload identity for every service
Traffic splitting by percentage: canaries and gradual rollouts
Retries, timeouts and circuit-breaking limits as config
Outlier detection: stop sending to a misbehaving pod
Metrics and trace spans for every request

shots.engineer: So what does the mesh give you without touching application code? Mutual TLS, with an identity for every workload. Traffic splitting by percentage, for canaries and gradual rollouts. Retries, timeouts and circuit-breaking limits, set as configuration. Outlier detection, which stops sending traffic to a pod that keeps failing. And metrics and distributed traces for every request. One caveat: tracing still needs the app to pass trace headers from incoming to outgoing calls.
shots.executive: Encryption, safe rollouts, retries and monitoring all come from configuration rather than from each team writing code.

shots.title: Bad pod
shots.engineer: Now one payments pod goes bad. The orders sidecar sends attempt one to pod A and gets a five-oh-three. It retries on pod B, which succeeds, and the app never sees the error. Meanwhile Envoy's outlier detection is counting. By default, five consecutive server errors eject a host from the load-balancing pool for thirty seconds, and the time grows each time it is ejected again. By default, no more than ten per cent of a cluster can be ejected at once.
shots.executive: When one copy of a service misbehaves, the mesh retries elsewhere and stops sending it traffic for a while, so users rarely notice.

shots.title: Retries multiply
shots.engineer: But retries can multiply. Istio's documented default retries an HTTP request twice, so three attempts. If the app still uses its old library and tries three times as well, one user request can become nine calls to a service that is already struggling. Add another layer and it multiplies again. Istio's own docs warn that app and mesh timeouts can also conflict. So pick one layer to own retries and timeouts, give them a budget, and turn the other off.
shots.executive: If both the service and the mesh retry, one failed request can turn into many, so only one of them should be in charge of retrying.

card.heading: Plumbing in the app, or in the mesh
points: Library in each service | Sidecar mesh
No extra hop | Two extra proxy hops per call
Memory only in the app | A proxy's CPU and memory per pod
One version per language | One proxy, any language
Change means redeploy | Change is config, pushed live
Nothing new to run | A control plane to run and upgrade

shots.engineer: The costs are real. Every call now passes through two extra proxies, one on each side, adding latency to every hop. Every pod carries a proxy that needs its own CPU and memory, which adds up across thousands of pods. And the control plane is another critical system to run, upgrade and debug. Microsoft says a sidecar may not be worth it for a small application, or where the platform already gives you the capability. In return, you get one implementation for every language, changed by configuration.
shots.executive: A mesh adds a little delay, extra computing cost and another system to run. In return, every service gets the same security and reliability.

shots.title: Sidecarless
shots.engineer: Because of that cost, newer meshes drop the per-pod proxy. Istio's ambient mode, generally available since version one point twenty-four in November twenty twenty-four, runs a ztunnel on each node for layer four: mutual TLS, authentication and telemetry. A waypoint proxy, which is Envoy, is added only where you need layer seven features. Cilium uses eBPF in the kernel for the network path, and a per-node Envoy for HTTP and gRPC. Fewer proxies to run, with a different way to debug.
shots.executive: Newer designs share one helper per machine instead of one per service, which cuts the cost while keeping most of the benefits.

card.heading: In the wild
points: Project | What it is
Envoy | C++ proxy built at Lyft · CNCF graduated
Istio | Envoy sidecars or ambient · CNCF graduated 2023
Linkerd | Rust micro-proxies · CNCF graduated 2021
Cilium | eBPF datapath, per-node Envoy
Kubernetes | Native sidecar containers, stable in v1.33

shots.engineer: In the wild. Envoy, originally built at Lyft, is a C++ proxy that runs beside each application and is the data plane for many meshes; it is a graduated CNCF project. Istio uses Envoy sidecars or ambient mode, and graduated in July twenty twenty-three. Linkerd uses its own Rust micro-proxies and graduated in twenty twenty-one. Cilium builds on eBPF. And Kubernetes now has native sidecar containers, stable since version one point thirty-three, which start before the app and stop after it.
shots.executive: Envoy, Istio, Linkerd and Cilium are the well-known open-source options, and Kubernetes now supports sidecars directly.

card.heading: Related patterns
points: Pattern | How it relates
API gateway | North-south traffic in; the mesh handles east-west
Retry and timeout | Configured in the mesh; own them in one layer
Circuit breaker | Proxy limits and outlier detection
Ambassador | A sidecar that proxies outbound calls only

shots.engineer: Its neighbours. An API gateway handles north-south traffic coming in; the mesh handles east-west traffic between services, and many systems run both. Retries and timeouts are patterns the mesh implements for you, but only if one layer owns them. Circuit breaking shows up as connection limits in the proxy and outlier detection. And the ambassador pattern is a sidecar that only proxies outgoing calls, often for legacy apps you cannot change.
shots.executive: The mesh works alongside a gateway at the edge, and it provides retries, timeouts and circuit breakers so services do not have to.

card.heading: Recap
points: Move network plumbing out of the code, into a proxy beside it
Proxies are the data plane; one control plane gives rules and identity
It costs hops, CPU and operations: own retries in one layer

shots.engineer: Three things to remember. Move networking plumbing, such as TLS, retries, timeouts and telemetry, out of every service and into a proxy that runs beside it, so every language gets the same behaviour. The proxies form the data plane, and one control plane hands them configuration and identity. And it is not free: it adds hops, CPU and memory, and a system to operate, so own retries in one layer, and consider sidecarless modes.
shots.executive: Take networking out of the code. Run it centrally from one control plane. Mind the cost, and do not retry twice.

meta.blurb: Move TLS, retries and telemetry out of every service into a proxy beside it, run centrally by one control plane.
